summary: Defines SNMP management objects that expose the operation of a RADIUS authentication client, so administrators can watch login requests. It was replaced by RFC 4668.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of meters on the machine that asks a server whether a person may log in, showing how often it asks and how it goes.

subtitle: Monitoring system objects for RADIUS authentication clients.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to monitor and troubleshoot RADIUS authentication clients (like network access servers) to see how well they are communicating with authentication servers.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a set of SNMP managed objects that expose the internal state and statistics of a RADIUS client, including how many requests it has sent, how many responses it received, and error counters.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can now use SNMP to query RADIUS clients and see metrics like authentication attempts, retransmissions, timeouts, and malformed responses. RFC 4668 replaced this standard.

facts.label: Managed objects
facts.value: 2 scalars and 1 table with 15 columns per row

today: RFC 2618 was a Proposed Standard for RADIUS client management. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4668, which updated the RADIUS client MIB.

sections.title: Monitoring RADIUS Clients
sections.content:
The RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) protocol is widely used in network access systems to authenticate users attempting to log in. A RADIUS client is typically a network access server (NAS) such as a router or dial-in server that sends authentication requests to a RADIUS authentication server on behalf of the user.

To manage these systems effectively, administrators need detailed information about how the client is operating: how many authentication requests it has sent, how many succeeded or failed, whether it is experiencing timeouts, and whether the responses from the server appear valid. This RFC defines a set of SNMP management objects (a MIB module) that expose these metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone tries to log into a network, a machine called a client asks a RADIUS server 'is this person allowed?' Administrators need to see whether that client is working well, so this standard lets them peek inside it.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework and MIBs
sections.content:
A Management Information Base (MIB) is a database of managed objects that can be monitored and configured using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). This RFC defines a MIB that is compliant with SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information Version 2), which provides a formal language for describing network management objects.

The RADIUS Client MIB defines two types of objects: scalars (single values like client identifier) and tables (arrays of related objects). The main component is the RADIUS Authentication Server Table, which contains one row for each RADIUS authentication server that the client communicates with. Each row holds statistics about the interaction between the client and that specific server.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is a way for a network manager to see what is happening inside machines on the network. A MIB is a list of things you can look at, like 'how many requests did you send' or 'did you get a bad answer back'.

sections.title: Client Statistics and Server Metrics
sections.content:
The MIB tracks several key objects at the client level, including the client identifier (NAS-Identifier) and a counter of invalid server addresses (authentication responses received from unknown servers). For each RADIUS authentication server, the MIB records the server's IP address and the UDP port the client uses to communicate with it.

The most important part of the MIB is a set of counters that track the lifecycle of authentication requests. These include the number of Access-Request packets sent, Access-Accept responses received (valid or invalid), Access-Reject responses, and Access-Challenge responses (requests for additional information). The MIB also counts retransmissions, timeouts, malformed responses, bad authenticators, and packets dropped for other reasons.

Additional metrics track round-trip time to the server, the number of pending requests (awaiting a response), and the number of unknown packet types received from the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The statistics show whether the client sent its request, whether the server answered, whether the answer looked correct, and whether things went wrong. There are separate counters for successes, rejections, challenges, timeouts, and corrupted messages.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that the RADIUS Client MIB contains no read-write or read-create objects, so SNMP clients cannot modify the configuration or state of the RADIUS client. However, certain objects are considered sensitive and should be protected from unauthorized access.

The most sensitive objects are the server IP address and port number. Revealing which server the client communicates with could help an attacker target the authentication server. The RFC recommends implementing SNMPv3 with its User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model to restrict which users can query these objects and to encrypt the values in transit. SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c provide no security, so SNMPv3 is strongly recommended for protecting this information.
sections.plainLanguage: The management objects are read-only, so no one can change them remotely. But the addresses and port numbers they contain could help someone attack the system, so you should use a secure version of SNMP (SNMPv3) to keep this information private.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC specifies that RADIUS authentication clients must implement this MIB if they are to be managed via SNMP. It is also possible for a RADIUS entity to act as both a client and a server (for example, in a RADIUS proxy that relays requests between clients and servers), in which case the entity should support both the client and server MIBs.

The MIB was designed to be translated to SMIv1 for compatibility with older SNMP implementations, though some features (such as 64-bit counters) cannot be represented in SMIv1 and are lost in translation.
sections.plainLanguage: If your RADIUS client wants to be managed by SNMP, it should provide this information. A machine that acts as both client and server should provide both the client and server statistics.
